rows.title: Breathe to three

transcript.eng:
Close your eyes. 

Use the magic power of three to stay connected and relax.

Breathe in to the count of three. 1, 2, 3. 
Breathe out to the count of three. 1, 2, 3. 
Breathe in to the count of three. 1, 2, 3. 
Breathe out to the count of three. 1, 2, 3.

Do you feel any different? Deep breathing helps our whole body and mind to calm down. 

You are a star!

text_1_facilitator.eng: Today’s topic is about what teens see online. Teens may come across videos, pictures, or messages that are confusing, upsetting, or not real. As parents, we can feel unsure how to talk about this. By staying calm and talking together, you can help your teen feel safe and make better choices online.

text_1_facilitator.eng: Many teens come across sexual content online, often without looking for it. Curiosity is normal, but what they see does not show real life or real relationships. They can feel confused, curious, or uncomfortable. When teens feel safe to talk, they are more likely to share. With your support, they can learn to think about what they see and understand what is real and respectful, and what healthy relationships look like.

text_1_facilitator.eng: Here are some simple ways you can support your teen when they see or share things online that are confusing or sensitive.

section_1_text.eng: It’s impossible to protect our teens from everything online, but some simple steps can reduce exposure. Set a family routine that all devices, including phones, must stay in common areas of the home, during the day and night. Set a strong example by following this rule yourself.

section_1_extra_text.eng: Connect with other parents to establish shared norms - it’s easier for teens to accept rules that their peers’ families also follow. Set up a communal spot for device charging that is outside of bedrooms.

section_2_text.eng: Not everything online is real. Videos, pictures, and sexual content can be made to get attention and may not show real life. Help your teen pause and think about what they see. Ask simple questions: Who made this? Why was it shared? Does it feel real?

section_2_extra_text.eng: Some people online may not be who they say they are. Remind your teen not to share personal details or sensitive content, and to talk to you or another trusted adult if they are unsure.

section_3_text.eng: Teens may feel pressure to share things quickly, especially when others are sharing. Remind your teen: if a friend sends a funny but sexual video, it’s okay to not pass it on. Your teen can say “I don’t send stuff like that.” Giving teens something clear to say reduces social pressure. Encourage your teen to pause before sharing anything online.

section_3_extra_text.eng: Remind your teen that sharing content can affect others and themselves. If something feels strange, unclear, or could harm others, it is safer not to share.

section_4_text.eng: If your teen sees something confusing or sexual online, stay calm and listen. This helps your teen feel safe to talk to you or another trusted adult. Thank your teen for telling you. Reassure your teen that they did nothing wrong. Avoid blame or anger.

section_4_extra_text.eng: Agree on simple rules together, like only using devices in shared spaces at home, to help your teen see less sexual content.

text_1_facilitator.eng: This week’s home activity is to talk with your teen about something they have seen online. Ask your teen to tell you about something interesting they saw online or something that felt confusing or strange. Remember to ask: What do you think about it? Do you think it is real? Why do you think it was shared? How can this affect others? Listen without judging and thank your teen for sharing.

quiz_1_question.eng: Can you talk with your teen about something they have seen online this week?

quiz_1_feedback_1.eng: That’s great! By staying calm and talking together, you help your teen feel safe to share and make better choices online.

quiz_1_feedback_2.eng: You can do it! Try asking your teen about something they have seen online. A simple “What have you been watching lately?” is a great way to start.

quiz_1_feedback_3.eng: That’s okay. This kind of conversation can feel hard at first. Remember, staying calm and showing interest helps your teen feel safe to talk.
